headings.text: **Fundamental Notion   (Organizing Observation About  Epistemic Principle About Economic Dimension of Social Reality)**

entries.text: 14.01 principles of microeconomics notes course goals - [ ] understand consumer and firm behavior. - [ ] analyze different types of market structures (monopoly, oligopoly and a competitive market). - [ ] apply economic principles to your daily life. - [ ] apply economic principles to solve a wide aspect of policy questions. - [ ] use supply and demand diagrams to analyze the impact of overall changes in supply and demand on price and quantity. - [ ] analyze the behavior of firms in a perfectly competitive market in the short-run and the long-run. - [ ] calculate producer and consumer surplus. a - [ ] analyze the behavior of firms in a monopoly or oligopoly, and calculate the resulting changes in producer or consumer surplus. - [ ] use economic tools to analyze economic policies. study calendar week topics suggested readings --- --- --- week 1: introduction and basic principles • what is economics?• opportunity costs• cost-benefit principle• the invisible hand principle• trade chapter 1 week 2: supply and demand • introduction• demand• supply• equilibrium• using the model chapter 3 week 3: market efficiency and government policies • consumer surplus• producer surplus• market efficiency• price controls chapters 4–5 week 4: elasticities • own-price elasticity of demand• own-price elasticity and total revenue• other demand elasticities• price elasticity of supply• application: taxes chapters 6–7 week 5: production and costs • the firm's production function• costs of production• economic profits chapter 11 week 6: competitive output • market structures• short-run competitive output• long-run competitive output chapter 12 week 7: firms with market power • monopoly• monopolistic competition• pricing with market power chapters 13 & 15 week 8: public goods, common resources, and externalities • public goods• common resources• externalities chapters 16–17 fundamental notion (organizing observation about epistemic principle about economic dimension of social reality) economic is looking at ‘economic decistion making’ - about production, consumption, etc - basically - when to produce, when to buy, at what price, etc - it’s an interaction theory according to this view - not production or technology. - which epistemic (research) social groups - that do epistemic activity fall into this? british economic tradition, marginalist school, austrian tradition, neoclassical economics, chicago school, public choice, new institutional economics, - which epistemic (research social groups - does not? german economic tradition, friedrich list, alexander hamilton, some marxist tradition (they were more about rage than positive things) -, evolutionary economics, technology studies. economic reality – interaction and decision-making - which is the epistemic scaffolding tools for (the derivation of the concrete epistemic artifact set ) used by this the researchers - in a recursive manner (principles → conception of market, etc)? - epistemic principles → market conception → actor model → interaction model → decision-making model → causal model → analytical framework → leaft concrete epistemic artifacts. (note a conceptual notion is a concerete epistemic artifacts - but usually not leaft - but root - used to create more concrete epistemic artifacts). - for neclassical tradition: methodological individualism + rational choice → market as a system of exchange → utility-maximizing agents → price-mediated interactions → optimization decisions → equilibrium causality → supply–demand and general equilibrium models → demand curves, elasticities, welfare analysis, market simulations, econometric models , etc. lectures week 1: introduction and basic principles - when people maximize their interest society wins. - the cost of doing something is the opportunity that is given up. - trade makes people better off. - rational people take an action only when the marginal net benefits of that action are positive. after you actively engage in the learning experiences in this module, you should be able to: - identify the main economic problem. - recognize situations in which the concept of the "invisible hand" plays a role in maximizing society’s welfare. - differentiate between marginal and average benefits of an activity. - identify what are the opportunity costs of a good or activity. - identify the benefits to each person or country engaged in trade. keep your eyes open for the following key terms or phrases as you complete the readings and interact with the lectures. these topics will help you better understand the content in this module. - marginal benefits and marginal costs - opportunity costs - specialization and trade - invisible hand develop your answers to the following guiding questions while completing the readings and working on assignments throughout the week. - why do we need economics? what is the main economic problem? - what are the opportunity costs of obtaining a good or engaging in an activity? - why should trade always lead to higher benefits to those involved? - what are the differences between marginal benefits (costs) and average benefits (costs)? entries.text: 18.01sc single variable calculus goals; improve my comprehensive understanding; improve my mental representations & functional mapping; in differentiation & integration. the art of solving integrals - it’s basically the art of finding representations for the differential function being integrated; a technique for this is called substitution. definition and basic rules in this module, we explore the differential operator — its definition in terms of the secant-line limit , its geometric interpretation as the tangent line, and the derivative of a function at a point $x 0$, denoted $f'(x 0)$. the derivative at $f'(x 0)$ is the slope $m$ of the tangent line (limit of the secant line) at $x 0$, $f(x 0 + \delta x) - f(x 0) = m (x 0 + \delta x - x 0)$ . note: most functions do not have a constant slope — they are not straight lines — meaning $\delta y \not\propto \delta x$ globally. instead, we work with local slopes : we examine the behavior near a chosen point $x 0$, compute the slope of the tangent line there, and use it as a local linear approximation. conceptually, this amounts to partitioning the curve into infinitesimal intervals and approximating each by its tangent line — creating an infinite collection of local linear models that together reconstruct the function’s behavior. note: the slope represents the rate of change of a function. it measures how much $\delta y$ changes per unit of $\delta x$, that is, how $\delta y$ is distributed across $\delta x$ at each point of the function. note: the concept of a limit captures the idea of approaching a value through infinitely many approximations. image.png image.png differentiable → continuous? reason about this logical pattern and the concepts mentioned above. limits: - what is the use of the concept? why the concept? which are the limits of the concept? what are the alternatives of the concept? entries.text: conduct of life index guiding questions: - how to ground the meaning of our life? - how to lift our “existence” thought our own means - by the interaction with others? group - co evolution through joint support. - how do we develop our imagination to problematize our existence and experiment with new possibilities? - how do we understand the otherness of other people? - which are the possible telos of philsophy? a super science, a guide to life, etc. - why are this telos risky? - which are the major themes or agenda of the course? - self-inventionn - responsability and solidatiry - which is the conception of the old concept of ethics? introduction see more in https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l88hd vls1m. how do we rethink human life and human experience? what grounds human existence? ordering of social relations in bronze age societies: hierarchical. born of salvationist religion → … → secular period. - the soul of another person is a dark continent that can never be fully explored. - author unknown . anglo-american philosophy conduct of life theories - deontology: rooted in immanuel kant's philosophy, it emphasizes following universal moral laws, often expressed as categorical imperatives. - consequentialism (utilitarianism): best exemplified by jeremy bentham, this position focuses on maximizing overall happiness or good, often summarized as "the greatest happiness for the greatest number". - contractualism: this approach, associated with jean-jacques rousseau, posits that moral principles arise from a social contract or agreement among rational individuals. references - ..

1. 25 2. 0.3412 3. 0.5 4. 0.25 5. 5.4 6. 0.4345 7. no the central limit theorem image.png 1. 0.471 2. 2 3. 5 4. 0.814 point estimation in this module, we introduce discrete random variables, the probability mass function (pmf), and the bernoulli distribution, indicator function, … distributions: bernoulli distribution, the geometric distribution, the binomial distribution, the poisson distribution. recognizing probability distributions - is a skill that i should practice. distribution description --- --- bernoulli models a single trial with only two possible outcomes: success (1) or failure (0), with probability of success $p$. geometric models the number of independent bernoulli trials needed until the first success occurs, with probability of success $p$. binomial models the number of successes in $n$ independent bernoulli trials, each with probability of success $p$. poisson models the number of events occurring in a fixed time or space interval when events happen independently at an average rate $\lambda$. gauss exponential continuous uniform gamma distribution chi-squared distribution transformation of distribution : let’s say that we have a random variable x that follows certain distribution d, and we apply operator to that random variable - including ones that deal with other random variable; how to derive the new distribution form $x d$ where d means derived? estimator: a rule or function that provides an estimate of a population parameter based on sample data. method of moments: a technique for estimating population parameters by equating sample moments (like mean, variance) to the corresponding theoretical moments of the distribution. maximum likelihood estimation - mle, invariant property, … large sample properties of maximum likelihood estimators see more here ‣. fisher information: how much information the data gives about the unknown parameter. it is based on how sensitive the likelihood is to changes in the parameter. cramér-rao lower bound: the smallest possible variance that any unbiased estimator of a parameter can have. it is a benchmark for efficiency. the weak law of large numbers: as the sample size gets bigger, the sample mean gets closer (in probability) to the true population mean. the central limit theorem: for large samples, the sample mean is approximately normally distributed, no matter the original distribution (if it has finite mean and variance). large sample properties of estimators: - consistent estimator: as the sample size grows, the estimator gets closer to the true parameter value. - asymptotically unbiased: any bias in the estimator disappears as the sample size grows. - asymptotically efficient: for large samples, the estimator has the smallest possible variance among all consistent estimators. confidence intervals involving the normal distribution references - https://www.coursera.org/specializations/statistical-inference-for-data-science-applications

entries.text: version control basics a two-lecture course on the ideas behind version control: why history matters, and the commit, branch, and merge workflow every tool implements. lectures 1. why version control? 2. commit, branch, merge references - pro git (entire book, cc-licensed)

entries.title: Lecture 1 — Why Version Control?

headings.text: What problem does version control solve?
What properties must a solution have?

entries.text: lecture 1 — why version control? before commands: the problems version control solves, and the properties every solution shares. formulation what problem does version control solve? collaborative editing over time: several agents change the same files, mistakes happen, and past states must stay recoverable. without history, the work exists only in its latest, most fragile form. what properties must a solution have? identity (every state addressable), history (states linked in order), branching (parallel lines of work), and merging (recombining lines). centralized and distributed tools differ only in where history lives. takeaway version control turns a pile of files into a queryable history of intentions — who changed what, when, and why .

entries.title: Lecture 2 — Commit, Branch, Merge
entries.text: lecture 2 — commit, branch, merge the core loop: record a snapshot, diverge safely, recombine deliberately. formulation what is a commit? an immutable snapshot with identity, parent pointer, author, and message. history is a linked list (usually a dag) of commits — the "why" lives in the message. what are branches and merges? a branch is a movable pointer to a commit: cheap divergence. a merge reconciles two lines of history into one, pausing for human judgment on conflicts. the loop — commit, branch, merge — is the same in every tool; only the storage model differs. takeaway branch to explore, commit to record, merge to agree. everything else is interface.
